title: 1999-02-21 MacWorld Tokyo 1999
speaker: Steve Jobs
content:
Good morning.

Thank you. Good to be here. So, my name is Steve Jobs. I'm the interim CEO of Apple. And we get to spend a little bit of time this morning. I've got four things that I'd like to talk about, if that's okay. So let's get started. Of course, the first one, the first one is our new Power Macintosh G3. I hope all of you've seen this by now. And I want to tell you some of the thinking that went into designing this. We had four goals for the product. The first was to be the most powerful Macintosh ever designed, and even beyond that, the most powerful PC ever, of any kind. The second goal was to have the best graphics in the industry, including the best real-time 3D graphics. The third goal was to be the most expandable personal computer ever made. And the fourth fourth goal was to have the best design of any personal computer. So let's go through these goals one by one. The first one, the most powerful. How did we do it? Well, these G3 ship with a four up to a 400 MHz Power PC processor. And this is the first processor ever to ship commercially using copper. So it's very, very fast. And let's see how fast. Well, in addition to the processor running at 400 MHz, we've got the cache is running at 200 MHz and the memory running at 100 MHz. And so when we compare these to the fastest Pentium 2 money can buy, the 450 MHz, right? In byte marks, that's 5.6. The old G3s did 11.3, and the new G3s do over 13 byte marks. So these are really, really fast boxes. And to give you a demonstration of how fast, I'd like Phil Schiller, our worldwide vice president of product marketing, to join me, and we're going to do a bake off.

Phil, where's Phil?

I need Phil. All right, Dave. Come on.

Thanks for joining. Okay, what have we got here, Phil?

And the demo we're going to show you today is of Adobe Photoshop, one of the most used applications in the professional market. And we've got a large Photoshop file created by one of our customers. And this is a real file that was created to do a real job. Now how big is the file, Phil?

And we're going to have the fastest PC money can buy and the new Power Mac G3 step through these things as fast as they can and see which one is the fastest. Now this is exactly the same file running on both computers. So let's go.

Select Photoshop here. Okay, ready to go?

I'll count us down. Three, two, one, go. Okay, there goes the Mac is off. The PC is thinking, thinking. The deep thinker. So here we go. You might begin to guess what this algorithm is from. And the Macintosh is done.

We're getting there.

Okay. Now, one of the things, let's run this again, Phil. Uh one of the things that graphic artists do a lot in Photoshop is they revert. So let's even measure the revert time.

Three, two, one, revert.

Now the Macintosh is giving us status here, it's it's reverting. The PC is just uh

Getting an hourglass. And uh the Macintosh is ready again. The PC is thinking. And thinking some more. Okay, there we go. So let's run this test again. Uh I'll count down. Three, two, one, go. I didn't push it. I'm giving him a head start. Okay, now, the Macintosh is done now.

We're ahead of him already.

Uh-huh. Exactly what it means. And the Mac is done.

So what we're seeing here is that the PC is 62% slower than the Macintosh, running Photoshop exactly the same file, the kind of things that our customers do every single day, many, many times per day. Thank you, Phil.

Okay. So we've made the most powerful PC that you can buy. The best graphics. Now, Macintosh has always had great 2D graphics, but we wanted to go and extend that to 3D graphics. And we bet on a new technology that was going to come out about the same time as the G3. And that technology is the ATI Rage 128 graphics accelerator. It's the fastest graphics accelerator ever made for a personal computer. And Macintosh is the first and so far only PC to use it. We've complemented it with 16 megabytes of graphics memory. So it's very, very fast and it can store large texture maps. Now, a lot of different markets need 3D graphics: education, science, websites, business. But the one thing that pushes 3D graphics the hardest is games. Games not only push the 3D graphics the hardest, but they also push the whole system performance the hardest. And so I'd like to show you how fast this really is. Now, in the PC market, none of the PC manufacturers build in good 3D graphics. So to get good 3D graphics, you have to add an add-in card. And the most popular one and the best one in the PC market is the Voodoo 2 card. And it costs an extra, thank you. It costs an extra $200. What we're going to do is take a look at what the graphics built in to every new Power Mac G3, how does that compare with even this extra $200 card? Well, the graphics from the prior generation G3 used a chip called the Rage Pro. And it would play the game Quake at 36 frames per second. The Voodoo 2 card running in a PC, a 450 MHz Pentium 2 PC, would run Quake at 50 frames per second. The new ATI Rage 128 built into every G3 model for no extra charge runs Quake at 68 frames per second. So what I would love to do now is show you that. So can I get Phil back out here? Okay.

So Phil, what have we got here?

Great. And we've got a new great game here called Dark Vengeance, one of the hottest new 3D games. And what we're going to do is we're going to run Dark Vengeance on both machines at the same time. And there's a sequence of of play events that this game is going to go through, and we're going to see which one gets done quickest.

You like to count us down to begin?

Three, two, one, go.

Now, it turns out that the Mac was able to render that game at 55 frames per second versus 45 frames per second on the fastest PC with a $200 Voodoo 2 add-in card. So you can see the difference in performance there. The Mac is 20% faster than even the Voodoo 2 card added into the fastest PC. Thank you, Phil.

Now, now that we've got the best hardware in the industry, we wanted to provide a graphics library, a 3D graphics standard in software for our developers. And we chose what we think is the best one out there after talking with our developers, which is OpenGL from Silicon Graphics. And we've licensed that, and we're going to be building OpenGL into all future releases of the Macintosh operating system. And I think the game developers are extremely excited about this. So, we think we've nailed the best graphics in the industry. The most expandable. Well, to start with, you can add up to a gigabyte of memory inside our new Power Mac G3s. And you can add 100 gigabytes of disk inside that box using three disk drives. We can hold up to three disk drives, and we will be shipping the new IBM 36 gig disk drives as our highest end build to order option. So you can have over 100 gigabytes of disk drives inside the box with these three drives. In addition to that, we've added a fourth slot. So there are now four slots inside, and three of them are 64-bit PCI for very, very fast peripherals. On the IO ports, let me explain our philosophy first. We believe in using industry standards. We believe in using IO that is serial versus parallel, because high-speed serial IO means much smaller cables, much nicer for consumers as well as professionals. And we believe in plug and play. You should be able to plug it together and it should just work. No switches to set or anything else. So what IO have we built in to the new Power Mac G3 that meets this philosophy? Well, of course, the first one is Ethernet. Ethernet is an industry standard. It is high-speed serial interface. And we have 100 megabit Ethernet built in, and you can get it now with gigabit Ethernet available in the new Power Mac G3, the first personal computer in the industry to offer it. The second thing we've built in is Universal Serial Bus. This is a new industry standard that is terrific. It's called USB for short, and this is its symbol. Now, what does USB do that the old serial ports in the Mac didn't do? A lot. Let me compare them. The old serial ports ran fairly slow. USB is 30 times faster at 12 megabits per second. The serial ports, you could connect two devices to your Mac. With USB, you can connect 127 devices to your Macintosh. The old serial ports were not hot pluggable. You needed to really turn off the power to do something safe with. USB, you can plug in and out with the power on and it automatically self-configures. And the drivers are dynamically loadable. So when you plug in a new USB device, the drivers will be dynamically loaded in. And it's an industry standard, which means that when a peripheral company wants to make a new peripheral, to make a version for the Mac, all they have to do is write the driver. The hardware is exactly the same as what they would use for Windows. So this is really great. And the number of USB devices is going through the roof. There are soon to be over 100 USB devices shipping for the Macintosh by the end of this quarter, by the end of next month, over 100 will be shipping. Next, we have built in FireWire. Apple invented this technology years ago, and the IEEE adopted it as a standard, IEEE 1394, a few years ago. There was a press release just issued yesterday, uh of many companies in the industry getting behind this, and it is really, really picking up momentum to be a very powerful industry standard in both the personal computer industry and the consumer electronics industry. This is the symbol for FireWire. And let me take you back and explain why we need it. When the Macintosh first shipped with a scuzzy port, it was 12 years ago, 1987. And it was a breakthrough. It was a high-speed parallel interface that connected to both the internal disk drives, but also external disk drives and other peripherals like scanners, etc. And it worked great. But that was 12 years ago.


---

## Part 2

What's happened since is that the scuzzy ports that Apple built in is only used for external devices, and much faster versions of scuzzy or other interfaces are used for internal disk drives.
So Ultra ATA, which is very fast, much faster than the old Apple scuzzy, is what we use to talk to disk drives in the new Power Macintosh G3.
And for the very high end, we use Ultra 2 scuzzy.
But this is different than the scuzzy that comes out the back.
The scuzzy that comes out the back is a bit of an orphan, and it's not so fast.
And so when we compare it to FireWire, let's take a look.
It is, FireWire is five times faster than the old scuzzy port that used to come out the back of a Macintosh.
FireWire can connect to 63 devices instead of just seven.
FireWire is hot pluggable.
So I can plug things in and out with the power on.
You should not do that with scuzzy.
You could destroy your devices and your computer.
You need terminators with scuzzy.
If you don't plug the terminators in correctly, you can get data corruption or it just won't work.
No such thing in FireWire.
There's no such thing as terminators, you can throw them away.
And no dip switches in FireWire.
In scuzzy, you got to set all these little switches just right, or it doesn't work.
None of this in FireWire, all automatic.
And so if you like this, if you like these big thick cables, and if you like the terminators, and if you like setting switches, well that's okay.
Because you can buy a scuzzy card and put it in your new Power Mac G3.
But if you don't want to do any of that stuff, you can use FireWire.
Nice thin cable, everything's automatic, it's much faster.
And so, as an example, Sony licensed FireWire from Apple several years ago and has made it the standard for digital video inside the digital camcorders.
There's a FireWire connector on over 4 million digital camcorders today, over half of them in Japan.
It is the industry standard for digital video.
And it is being adopted by more and more personal computer devices and consumer electronics devices.
So, let me give you an example of how this stuff works.
I have some FireWire devices over here.
First of all, I have a Kodak digital camera.
Like most digital cameras, most high-end digital cameras, it has a FireWire jack here that I can just plug right in to my new Power Mac G3.
I've got a box that Sony sells that has analog video in and FireWire out, so that I can get analog video in and out through FireWire by this very inexpensive box from Sony.
I've got a magneto-optical drive by Yano, which is shipping next month, so I can store up to 500 megabytes of removable magneto-optical storage with a FireWire interface.
But one of the most exciting things is video.
And I've got a video camera here with a FireWire jack on it, and I'll just show you how this works.
I've just got some FireWire cables here, and it's very easy.
You just literally, the power's on, I've got a Power Mac G3 and the camera, they're both turned on.
And when I plug this in, FireWire will take a few seconds to automatically configure itself, figure out what's going on, and put the video on the screen.
So let me just do that.
So I plugged it in, and in a few seconds, I should come up here.
There I am, right there.
Hi, Mark.

And what I can do is I can just unplug it, right?
It stops.
I plug it back in like this, a few seconds later, I should be live again.
There I am.

Unplug it, right?
Very simple.
So let me plug it back in again.
And so now I've got some video here.
But FireWire is more than just a point-to-point interconnection.
It's a bus, which means I can plug multiple devices together on the same FireWire.
So what I'm going to do now is I'm going to take that same FireWire, and I'm going to plug it into a second G3, which is up here, and I'm going to feed both of them with the same signal off the FireWire from the digital camera.
So here I am right here now, and I'm going to plug in my second one right now, and it's going to take about three seconds to reconfigure, and hopefully in three seconds I'm up on both.
There I am.

And now I'll unplug it, and it'll freeze, but now here I am over here again on this one, right?
I'll plug it back in, and in a few seconds, I should be up on both.
Okay.
Whoops.
So, let me quit out of this application, and let me show you one last thing.
One of the things that our customers do a lot in the publishing and design market is they have such large files that they use external hard disk drives as sneakernet to carry giant files between computers in the same office or between computers in different offices across town, or even taking them on airplanes to different cities, right?
Have you ever done that?
A lot of people do that.
And it's a pain, because you got to have a big hard drive, you've got to plug it in for power, etc.
No more.
And of course, you have to turn your computer off before you plug it in, and you have to turn your computer off before you unplug it, right?
No more.
This is a new 4 gigabyte drive that will be shipped next month.
It has two FireWire ports on it.
It fits in your pocket.
And not only does it communicate with FireWire, but FireWire from the computer has power on it, so it's powered by the FireWire.
So watch this.
I'll take my FireWire here, and I will plug it into the disk drive, like this.
The disk drive is starting to spin up now, and in a second, there we go.
Okay?

And let me go ahead and launch some data off it.
I've got a QuickTime movie on here, so let me go ahead and launch that.
It's coming off the hard drive.

[Music playing]

Now, I'll unplug it.
I'll unplug this and as soon as the QuickTime buffer fills out, it'll stop.
Okay?

So, this is a small example of some of the dozens of FireWire devices that are coming on the market now and very soon, and we are extremely excited about FireWire.
Now, once you get video into the computer, you'd like to edit it.
And Apple is going to be coming out with some really cool video editing software in the next few months called Final Cut.
And we are demoing that out in our booth and I would invite you to take a look at it.
It's really great.
So, most expandable.
Again, we have up to a gigabyte of memory, 100 gigabytes of disk, CD-ROM, DVD, zip drives that you can put into these new machines, four slots with 64-bit PCI, Ethernet up to a gigabit per second, USB with up to 127 hot pluggable devices, FireWire with up to 63 hot pluggable devices.
And we think we've built the most expandable Macintosh ever.
Lastly, best design.
I know many of you have seen this already, but we are extremely pleased with the design of the new G3.
It's very, very elegant, and it really changes your idea about what a mini tower could look like.
In addition, there's this magic latch on the side that when you open it, opens the whole side door of the product to give you access to everything, and the computer is even still running.
It's very, very revolutionary if you need to get inside your computer frequently.
We also have a whole new series of displays that are quite beautiful.
And so, we think we've achieved the best design for this class of a product ever.
And let me show it to you in person here.
Let's get the video on, please.
So here we have it right here, and let me just go ahead and open it for you.
We can just grab this and open it right like this, and you see the whole product right here.
Come on around to the side.
We've got our memory here, our processor, our FireWire, we've got four IO slots here, we've got our three disk drives here, we have a removable storage up here.
And again, you can just close it, open it, and close it.
And there's a security thing on the back where if it's Isn't that great?

Our engineers worked for almost a year to figure out how to do this just right.
And there's even a way to lock it on the back so that nobody can get into your computer if you don't want them to.
So we think we've got, we think we've achieved the best design ever for this class of a product.
So our four goals, again, most powerful, best graphics, most expandable, and best design, and we think we've really achieved these four goals for this wonderful new product.
We actually had a fifth goal too, which was the best value.
We've brought our pricing down significantly to where you can buy one of these new G3s for a little over 200,000 yen, and we are very, very proud of this as well.

So, we made a video that I'd love to show you on the product.
It's called The Look of Love.
So if we could roll that now.

We set out to make a computer just for our pro customers.
From the ground up, we asked ourselves, what do they want?
What do they want for performance?
What do they want for expansion?
What do they want for features and industrial design?
What do they want for the whole system?
To try and design, design an object that elicits the reaction of, I really want that.

I can hardly wait to hold you, feel my arms around you
These machines are beautiful, but they kick ass.
We're building the fastest machines in the PC industry.
So we start with 400 megahertz processor with one megabyte backside cache, up to a gigabyte of high performance memory.
It supports the technologies that we've been trying to use for a long time now anyway, fiber channel, 64-bit PCI bus, 66 megahertz PCI bus.
I have not seen any other machine, any other platform have that kind of performance.
If sex is power and the computer gives you power, there's lots of sex in these machines.
Gamers are looking for performance.
Games today have realistic environments that are generated by tons and tons of polygons.
So we need the most advanced machines out there to make the games look great.
The brand new ATI Rage 128, this is the fastest graphic accelerator available, and it's in the Macintosh first.
The Rage 128 hardware is among the best available anywhere.
It delivers very good performance, extremely good quality.
This platform will deliver several times better performance than anything else that's available on the Macintosh world.
With the new G3, we broke the laws of physics.
We actually put more features, more expandability into a smaller box.
So we designed it so one flip of a lever and the whole door opens, you have full accessibility to the enclosure.
To make it really easy to add memory, to make it really easy to add IO cards.
No special tools, it's all right there.
Handles to pick it up, a door to get inside, what a great thought, and it's the Apple system.
The professional is going to want access to the IO capacity.
The thing has got every real fast technology that's on the market today.
Ultra ATA 33, FireWire, USB, 100 megabit Ethernet, all on the motherboard now.
If you want a future of IO, it's USB and FireWire.
You don't have to worry about cable lengths, you don't have to worry about terminations, you don't have to worry about device select addresses.
You just plug it in and it works.
I mean 127 devices on USB, 63 devices on FireWire.
It's the easiest thing in the world.
I just take this camera, a simple FireWire cable, I plug it into my Power Mac G3, and digitally take that video onto my computer and bam, I'm editing video and I'm on my way.
It's got to be absolutely compelling with the performance in terms of raw speed and power, but also these have to be objects that are totally seductive.
We designed a new family of Apple Studio Displays to go along with the new G3.
There's a 21-inch monitor that is the dream publisher's monitor, Trinitron, color management, digital color calibration, USB hub for peripherals.
The 17-inch monitor that has the best quality in the business, and still very affordable.
And the award-winning 15-inch Apple Studio Display.
The stand floats the display in space, put air underneath, it makes it appear lighter.
Rock solid and crisp and sharp, and you just love it.
We had to make a powerful machine, we had to give our customers tremendous features, we had to make it gorgeous.
We also had to make it really affordable.
When customers see the new technology and they see the new design, they're going to be all over these machines.
When I see this thing, I'm going to not.
They're going to want it.
Still doing the fastest machines in the industry is great.
So that's what drives us.
We're putting them right in the furnace.
It is close.

A computer absolutely can be sexy.

So, that is our new Power Macintosh G3, and that's the first thing I wanted to talk about today.
The second, second of course, is iMac.
We are so thrilled with the reception that iMac has had in Japan and around the world.
It's been great.
Thank you very much.

iMac went on sale August 15th.
And as you know, last year ended on December 31st, and so the question we got asked a lot was, how many iMacs did you sell in the first four and a half months of the product's life?
And the answer is 800,000.

That's one every 15 seconds during that time period.

And that has made iMac the number one computer in America, and it's made iMac the number one computer in Japan.

And that's made us very happy.
So, we do a lot of market research at Apple, and we just got back our December research.
And the question is, who is buying iMacs in Japan?
And let me share that with you now.
It's pretty amazing.
The most important thing when you're selling a consumer computer is how many first-time computer owners are buying your product.
How many first-time owners are coming to the Macintosh?
Because these are the most important customers.
They expand our installed base, and they're choosing Macintosh as their first computer.
And the industry average is in the mid-20%.
And with iMac, it's 46%.

46% of Japanese buyers of iMacs are first-time computer owners.
Another 16% are Wintel converts.

And that means that 62% of the iMacs being bought are added to Apple's installed base.
This is incredible for not only Apple, but for our software developers.
A much larger installed base to sell into.
And of course, that leaves 38% are existing Macintosh users.
So we could not be happier with these statistics in Japan.
Now, I'd like to share with you some other research.

## Part 3

**Steve Jobs**: that is integrated all over the world, Europe, Japan, the United States. Are you connected to the internet? The iMac customer base, 82% of them say they are connected to the internet. This is over double the industry average. Okay? Now, when did you get connected? Two thirds said the first day. How long did it take you to set up your iMac and get connected to the internet and access the internet? 44% said 15 minutes or less. That went up to 62% for 30 minutes or less, and to 74% for 60 minutes or less. Again, iMac is the easiest computer in the world to set up and access the internet. Have you purchased any goods over the internet? 42% said yes. And which search engine do you use most regularly? Again, this was what we got. Yahoo was number one, AOL was number two, AltaVista was number three, but look at number four. Sherlock was tied with Netscape. Now, Sherlock, for those of you that don't know, is a technology that we shipped in our last OS release, Mac OS 8.5 in October. So it's only been out there at this point for three months, and it's tied with Netscape for the fourth most popular search engine. We're very excited about this. Now, new iMacs for 1999, as you know, we upped the processor speed, we put a larger disc drive in, and we lowered the price to 158,000 yen. But most important, we got them in color.

Age of Empires, Myth 2, which is going to be very strong.
And the newest release of Quake.
The newest release of Quake, Quake as you know is authored by a man named John Carmack.
Brilliant, brilliant man.
And he pushes games farther than almost anybody.
And when we launched the Power Macintosh G3 last month in California, John Carmack himself came on stage and did a demo of the upcoming Quake Arena, which will be released simultaneously on the Mac and on Windows this spring.
And I am going to show you the demo that he brought to us.
I wish he could see it today.
And it's pretty amazing.
Okay.
This demo takes about a minute and a half and it's going to show us one of the most aggressive, it's going to show us one of the most aggressive things in the 3D that that we've ever seen on a computer using 3D real-time graphics.
We'll let it get started up here.
You're going to see reflections and fog and mist like we've never seen before.
Take a look at this.
Quake 3 Arena.
And the quality of the graphics are stunning using the new Rage 128 and OpenGL.
This is all based on OpenGL.

We've never seen this quality in games before.

Do you think this is cool?

You like it?

This is the second time this has ever been shown in public.
The first was at MacWorld last month.
Look at the reflection in the mirror there.
Again, never before been done in gaming.

Look at this mist.
Again, very difficult effect to do in real-time 3D graphics.
Very computationally intensive.

So this is the future of high-end gaming and you're going to see it first and you're going to see it best on the Macintosh.

Now, we're putting a lot of energy to bring the best games in the world to the Macintosh platform.
But we also want the most games in the world.

And the most games in the world are on the Sony PlayStation.
There's a company in California called Connectix, which has invented some software which allows you to go buy a Sony PlayStation game at the store, bring it home and actually play it on your Macintosh.
This software was announced last month at MacWorld and is shipping in the US today.
And we hope to see it in Japan by this summer or early fall.
And to give us a demo of this, I'd like to ask Phil to come back out.

Phil.

So, we always have the best games.
We hope to have the most games.
And that's the third thing I wanted to talk about today.
Fourth thing, Mac OS.
One of the things that is really wonderful is that we have one of only two high-volume operating systems in the whole world at Apple.
And we can really put a lot of energy into advancing our operating system forward.
And we've been doing that a lot with Mac OS 8.
As you know, our latest release was released in October, Mac OS 8.5.
It was a must-have upgrade.
If you haven't bought it, I strongly suggest you get it.
It's got some incredible features like Sherlock, much faster, five times faster AppleScript, much better ColorSync, and network copying that is now faster than NT.
So if you're in design and publishing or any other customer segment, we believe that Mac OS 8.5 is a must-have upgrade.
Shipped in October '98, we sold over a million upgrades to date, and coupled with the machines we've shipped, there are over 2 million copies of it out there already in approximately 90 days.
So we're very happy with the reception.
Everybody seems to think it's pretty great.
We're also working on future generations of the Mac OS.
And the next big one is called Mac OS 10, that you may be familiar with.
We are going to ship our first Mac OS 10 product this month in the US and in April here in Japan.
And that is Mac OS 10 Server.
We've taken the core OS and we're going to ship it as a server and it's a dynamite server.
And let me take you through what this is.
First of all, we start off with a very powerful operating system kernel called Mach.
And to that we add Macintosh File Service so that you can have files on the server that you can download to clients transparently.
In addition to that, we're adding a really cool feature to the server called NetBooting, to where you can have an iMac as a client, say, and you can actually boot off a copy of the operating system on the server.
Now, why would you ever want to do that?
Because you can have just one copy of the operating system on one server and serve as many Macs as you want.
And if you update that operating system, you change only one copy in one place and every user takes advantage of it.
The same reason you put files on a file server.
If you have a copy of AppleWorks on a file server and you update it once, everybody who then launches that application gets the updated copy.
In addition to File Service and NetBooting, we want this to be a dynamite web server and it is.
It's a very, very high-performance web server and we have added Apache, which is the number one web server software package in the world.
Over half the websites in the world use Apache as their web server.
Ours at Apple do.
And it's very good.
And to create applications which can run on Apache, we are bundling in a copy of our extremely powerful WebObjects software that has been used by over 3,000 corporations now and is the best application server for writing web applications, we believe, in the world.
In addition to that, for people that want to write very sophisticated custom apps, we've included Berkeley 4.4 Unix and Java.
And so this is Mac OS 10 Server.
We think it's very, very comprehensive and we're going to price it very attractively.
We're going to ship it in Japan localized in Japanese in April.
